opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap is taste. The current models are remarkably good at the execution layer of research: if you hand them a well-specified problem, say "implement this ablation" or "find the bug in this training loop" or "summarize what's been tried on this benchmark," they're often faster and more thorough than a strong grad student. But choosing *what* to work on is a different skill, and that's where they still feel pretty weak to me.

Part of it is that the models are trained to be agreeable and to produce the consensus view. If you ask one what the promising directions are in, say, robot learning, you'll get a very reasonable list: scaling data, better world models, sim-to-real, foundation models for manipulation. That's not wrong, but it's basically the median of what's on arXiv. Good research directions are almost by definition somewhat contrarian. You're betting that something most people think is a dead end, or haven't noticed yet, is actually going to work. The models are pulled toward the center of the distribution, and the interesting ideas live in the tails.

The second thing is that they don't have a strong sense of what's *tractable right now*. A lot of research taste is knowing "this idea is good, but it's five years too early because the compute isn't there," or "this idea was tried in 2016 and failed, but the reason it failed no longer applies." That requires a kind of causal model of why things worked or didn't. The papers don't really encode that, because people don't write up the real reasons their thing didn't work. A lot of that knowledge lives in hallway conversations and in people's heads.

And third, I'd say they lack skin in the game. When a researcher picks a direction, they're committing a year or two of their life, so they have a very visceral sense of risk and payoff. The models don't feel the cost of a wasted year, so their suggestions tend to be either too safe or vaguely ambitious without a concrete first experiment that would tell you quickly whether you're on to something. The best researchers I know are really good at finding that cheap, decisive first experiment, and I haven't seen models do that consistently yet.

That said, I don't think any of this is fundamental. You could imagine training on actual research trajectories, rewarding models for proposing directions that later turned out to matter, and I'd expect that gap to close faster than people think.

r001.rationale: The response says models struggle to choose research directions, but does not identify difficulty recognizing when an experimental track should be reconsidered.

r002.rationale: It mentions debugging a training loop as an execution task, but says nothing about Claude, infrastructure bugs, or reliance on a human to formulate the investigative question.

r003.rationale: It suggests training on research trajectories and rewarding consequential proposals, but does not propose reinforcement learning environments that incentivize lateral thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot because at 1X we're basically trying to figure out what research to do with a finite number of people and GPUs, and I've tried pretty hard to get models to help with that part, not just the execution.

The first thing I'd say is that they're really good at generating research directions that are locally plausible. You ask "what should I try next to improve policy generalization" and you get a tidy list: more data diversity, better augmentation, co-training with web data, some kind of world model. None of it is wrong. But it's all stuff that's already the consensus. It reads like the related work section of the median paper from the past year. What they're bad at is the thing that actually matters in choosing a direction, which is having a strong opinion about what's going to turn out to be true that most people don't yet believe.

And I think the reason is pretty structural. The models are trained on the published record, and the published record is heavily biased toward things that worked and toward the stories people tell after the fact about why they worked. What's missing is all the negative results, all the taste that lives in people's heads about "I tried that in 2019 and it was a disaster for reasons that have nothing to do with the paper that claims it works." So the model's prior over what's promising is basically the prior of someone who's read everything and run nothing.

The second failure is around what I'd call the cost side of the ledger. Choosing a research direction isn't just "what would be cool if it worked," it's "what would be cool if it worked, divided by how expensive it is to find out." The models have a really poor sense of that denominator. They don't know that a particular idea is going to take three months because your data pipeline doesn't support it, or that the evaluation is the hard part, or that there's one engineer on the team who could pull it off and they're busy. Humans who are good at picking directions are constantly doing that arithmetic, usually implicitly, and the models just don't have access to the state of your org.

Third thing, and this one is a bit more subtle: they're not good at noticing which questions are about to become irrelevant. A lot of research taste is just anticipating that some capability is going to fall out of scale or out of someone else's work in six months, so you shouldn't spend your time on it. The models tend to treat the research landscape as static. They'll suggest something that was a great idea eighteen months ago, before some lab already basically solved it, because from the text alone it still looks like an open problem.

And then the last one, which I'm actually the most interested in, is that they don't really commit. If you push a model on a direction and say "are you sure," it folds instantly. A good researcher will sometimes be wrong but will defend a bet for long enough to actually find out. The sycophancy stuff isn't just annoying in a chat window, it's actively bad when the task is to form a conviction and then go spend real resources on it. You want something that will argue with you.

So to be clear, I use them for this constantly, and they're a great brainstorming partner and an amazing way to quickly map out what the field thinks. But if I ask "what should we do," I'm still getting the average of the literature, and the whole point of choosing a direction is to not be the average.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re much better at answering a question than deciding which question is worth answering. If you give a model a well-defined problem, it can suggest techniques, connect ideas, and help you work through the details. But choosing a research direction requires judging which assumptions are wrong, which experiments will actually distinguish between hypotheses, and which problems are both important and tractable.

If you ask for research ideas, you often get things that sound like research proposals. They have the right vocabulary and a plausible motivation. But then you ask, “What’s the cheapest experiment that would convince you this idea is wrong?” and the answer is often much less compelling. That’s a useful test of whether there’s a substantive idea underneath the presentation.

The other missing piece is sustained contact with the problem. A researcher tries something, encounters a surprising failure, and changes their sense of what matters. Their taste develops through that feedback. A model in a chat interface can imitate the resulting judgment, but it doesn’t necessarily have that ongoing loop of making bets and learning from what happens. I think that loop is a big part of what makes someone good at choosing directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re much better at answering a well-posed question than deciding which question is worth asking. You can ask for ten research directions, and they’ll give you ten plausible directions. But plausibility is a pretty low bar. What you want is a sense of taste: this problem looks unfashionable, but there’s something important here, and this particular experiment could tell us whether it’s real.

Part of the difficulty is that the literature doesn’t contain all the information a scientist uses. It contains the polished story after something worked. It contains much less about the experiments that failed, the assumptions people quietly stopped believing, or why somebody spent six months pursuing a seemingly insignificant anomaly.

The models can recombine ideas from papers, and that’s useful. Where I find them less convincing is making a sustained bet under uncertainty. Why this direction rather than the other hundred things you could work on? What result would make you abandon it? What’s the cheapest experiment that would actually change your mind? That’s a much harder standard than producing a research proposal that sounds good.
